items.title: Capitalism, as Told by Its Enemies (The Dispatch, Phil Magness)
items.text:
**We return to the belabored c-word... (no, not the *cunts*...)**

New entry up on the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP), and it's a complete farce.

![](https://m.stacker.news/152774)

> Cordelli’s article is loaded with content from the Marxist or socialist far left. Space devoted to critics of capitalism far outpaces even basic descriptions of the economic concept, and proponents of capitalism are reduced to shallow parodies.

## "Cordelli’s prose functions as an anti-capitalist advocacy piece rather than a neutral and descriptive encyclopedia entry."

> Instead of attempting some semblance of balance, the new SEP entry author Chiara Cordelli, a professor of political philosophy at the University of Chicago, used this platform to air her own personal grievances with capitalism as an economic system

> Such imbalances could only emerge from an academic environment in which an ideological echo chamber supplants rigorous peer review, and the fashionable socialist perspectives of the professoriate lead it to mistake bad caricatures of a market economy for descriptive fact.

## "In an era when academia is under fire for a well-documented leftward ideological shift as well as declining standards of scholarly rigor, the publication of an encyclopedia entry with a pronounced anti-capitalism skew only confirms the public’s declining trust in our university system."

yup, just exit academia already https://stacker.news/items/1419510, https://stacker.news/items/1087308

***

Heavy skew in the supporting article/authors: of 169 authors cited half are outright hostile, 8% supportive; for the "Socialism" entry, it's two-thirds of 160 extremely supportive and only *two* overtly critical.
Maybe, just, *maybe* you're failing to live up to the standards of an "encyclopedia"

> In addition to the Marxists, Cordelli’s entry gives ample space to a stream of non-Marxian socialist and anti-capitalist thinkers such as the sociological historian Karl Polanyi, the far-left economist Thomas Piketty, and self-citations to Cordelli’s own writings in the “democratic socialist” tradition.

ridiculous. Word counts, too, excessively skewed toward negative accounts/criticism:

> The author was clearly more concerned with highlighting every minute facet of anti-capitalist academic writing imaginable than with helping readers understand what the concept means, or the reasons that people defend it.

and, ooops:

> Whatever criticisms may be offered of capitalism, **its underlying economic theories have coincided with an unparalleled rise in prosperity and well-being between the late 18**<sup>**th**</sup> **century and today**, often known as the [Great Enrichment](https://egc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2023-06/HOW%20ACATO%20VERSION%20May%20%2723%20final.pdf). By comparison, the Marxist perspectives that dominate Cordelli’s work carry the ignominious baggage of mass atrocity and economic ruin in the 20<sup>th</sup> century, though the phrase “Soviet Union” never appears in her entry.

***

ALSO, and this will shock the stackers, she's repeatedly *incorrect* in her entry text:

> Almost all the sources used to defend free markets are given superficial treatment, and even those superficial references tend to be wrong. She gives short shrift to economist Friedrich Hayek's work, yet manages to misrepresent those positions that she does discuss, such as when she depicts him as a theorist of equilibrium instead of as a theorist of coordination and information, which are distinct and often contradictory approaches.
> In an [illustrative thread](https://x.com/ben_golub/status/2087755449441399169) on X, Ben Golub, a professor of economics at Northwestern University, identified a number of other basic factual errors in the entry, such as the author’s claim that Hayek and Milton Friedman believed that, for capitalism to exist, “there must be complete, private, and unregulated markets for all ‘factors of production,’ including capital and labor,” despite both making allowances for regulation and market rules.

## The labor theory of value just assumed

> Cordelli also opens the first section of her entry with Marx's definition of capitalism and makes reference to the “labor theory of value” without acknowledging that this concept has been considered obsolete by mainstream economists since the 1870s.

yesyes, we know: Marxian economists *still* thinks this is a reasonable and valuable approach https://stacker.news/items/1471628

> Yet Cordelli proceeds as if Marx’s economic theories remain intact, ultimately devoting some 800 words spread across two different sections of the entry to exegesis on “surplus value.” That’s more verbiage on a single debunked Marxian concept than she provides to the entirety of Friedman’s work.

## "This is a philosophical equivalent of treating geocentrism or flat-earth theory as valid and useful ideas."

***

**Another world is possible**

> a better entry might include serious engagement with the Scottish Enlightenment precursors to the emergence of market capitalism in the late 18<sup>th</sup> century, with references to David Hume’s work on [trade](https://davidhume.org/texts/empl2/jt) and [currency](https://davidhume.org/texts/pld/bt), as well as something more than superficial references to Adam Smith.
> It might also discuss how the ideas we call “capitalism” came to supplant an older mercantilist economic order that used government policies to steer an economy for nationalistic objectives.

\== "As it stands, this rich and complex academic literature receives nary a mention beyond a few passing citations."

This is a pretty basic and reasonable ask:

> Since capitalism is fundamentally an economic concept, one could reasonably expect to see mainstream economic voices discussed, and competently so, by someone versed in economic theory. There would be a clear description of how profits work both as signals of demand and incentives for entrepreneurship, how competition between firms disciplines market actors, how market prices make economic calculation possible by signaling the relative scarcity of goods in a common denominator, and how government policies contribute to the creation of monopolies
> Welfarist arguments for capitalism would not be confined to a single paragraph, and would describe in detail how free-market capitalism has been responsible for lifting the world out of poverty. The way that capitalism incentivizes entrepreneurship, and the role entrepreneurs play in arbitrage and the creation of new goods and services, would play a more important role than the entry’s single paragraph on Joseph Schumpeter, the first economist to make entrepreneurship central to the understanding of economic development and change.

I don't know why people keep insisting on fairytales... Ms Cordelli, Mr. Beckert, Mr. Piketty et al -- have you guys tried feeling differently?

also, [Handre's tweet summary](https://x.com/Handre/status/2089619556272677056) was excellent:

![](https://m.stacker.news/152773)

> The word "capitalism" smuggles in the assumption that without deliberate institutional design, voluntary exchange produces exploitation. We tacitly accept that assumption every time we use the word uncritically.

items.title: Pleb Economist #13: ColdCard and the Law of Large Numbers
items.text:
This recent ColdCard incident highlighted a vulnerability in Bitcoin that we always knew about---weak entropy---but it also reminded me of a more subtle weakness, a weakness that I also consider to be the biggest vulnerability in the entire discipline of economics.

And that's reliance on the **Law of Large Numbers**.

I remarked in https://stacker.news/items/1536440/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1536680 that one of the **security assumptions** that made me feel comfortable using popular and seasoned hardware wallets is the notion that "if there was a major flaw, it would have been discovered by now."  It's on that assumption that I'm willing to adopt things that are popular and have been around for a while, and also why I'm slow to update.  The older version is more battle-tested, in my mind.

But the ColdCard scenario tests that assumption.  The vulnerability, once explained, is not that hard to understand (https://stacker.news/items/1536739/r/SimpleStacker).  The software had an if/else conditional that took the seed generation down the wrong path, never calling for hardware generation which uses noise in the physical environment, and instead falling back to its pre-defined, low-entropy software generation.  The question is **how did no one catch it for so long?**

The answer has to be: [not enough people were actually looking at it](https://stacker.news/items/1536478/r/SimpleStacker?commentId=1536686).  Bitcoin is a small community, and everyone is busy with their own things.  Very few people are spending the time to audit code.  You'd think the company has the responsibility, *and it does*, but the company itself probably only has a handful of engineers, all of whom are also busy, and if internal processes aren't correct, then these things can easily slip through the cracks.

Make no mistake though, this definitely looks like a failure on ColdCard's part.  Personally, I can't imagine not having a test to actually test whether the build is pulling entropy from physical signals, and whether the firmware actually routed the seed generation down the correct path.

But I digress.  The point is that, a lot of assumptions that we make rely on a critical mass of people actually doing something that you'd think they're incentivized to do.  But that's often not a good assumption.  Even if the incentive is there, there may be fewer people doing it than you think, at any given moment.

It's the same thing in economics. The classical arguments for why competitive markets are efficient rely on the Law of Large Numbers. They assume that there are enough people out there competing that bad actors can't get away with their bad actions for long.  Company is out there scamming customers or providing bad product?  Economists assume that there are thousands of potential competitors out there ready to jump into the opening left by the terrible company.  But reality isn't so simple.  At any given moment, you could probably count on one hand the number of people paying enough attention, and with enough capital and know-how to actually fill the gap.

Same with the Efficient Market Hypothesis. That's the idea that you can't beat the market, because the market price of any security on the stock market already contains all the relevant information.  But how true is that, really?  It's probably a decent approximation for heavily traded ETF baskets; but probably not for individual companies, especially smaller ones.  For those, there are likely a small number of people with better information who haven't acted on it yet, perhaps waiting for an opportune moment, or perhaps just having not spent their attention on it just yet.

This way of thinking has led to the classic joke: "Milton Friedman and Eugene Fama are walking down the street. Friedman sees a hundred dollar bill on the floor and says, 'Look, Eugene, someone left a hundred dollar bill!'  Fama, without looking down, says, 'Nonsense! If there was a hundred dollar bill lying around, someone would have taken it alraedy!'"

So you see, assumptions that everyone is always relentless optimizing at any moment, and that there are enough people out there doing rational things that all the rational things always get done instantly, is generally not a very good assumption.  Yet, economists rely on it for their models.  And, more relevant for this crowd: Bitcoiners can sometimes rely on it for their security assumptions.

It comes into play when Bitcoiners address questions about things like nation state attacks, like in this [famous Antonopoulos video](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/P3K70rkaCJc).  He assumes that we don't have to worry about a nation state attack because enough Bitcoiners will be ready to respond to it properly, and in a coordinated fashion.  He's right that if we did respond this way, it wouldn't be a huge concern.  But would we really be able to?  Will enough people be paying attention?  The nation state attacker would probably run enough psyops to seed doubt in the community as to what's really going on.  The number of actors prepared to act in their best interest at any given moment may be smaller than you think.

So that's the point I was trying to make.  Bitcoin relies on game theoretic security.  Game theoretic security relies on assumptions about how people behave according to their incentives.  No one denies that people *do* act according to their incentives.  But most game theoretic models assume a level of rationality that just isn't realistic.  Most people are not paying attention all the time.  The number of people who will act according to the model at any given moment is probably small.  The model may predict directions of movement over time fairly well, but "predicting direction over time" is not a good rubric with which to measure security.

In that sense, even though the ColdCard incident is a failure of the company, not Bitcoin, it also calls into question how we should think about macrosecurity in the Bitcoin system as a whole.

items.title: The Forest Reunion - How I lost my passion for music.
items.text:
The following probably shares more personal information about parts of my life than the reader may care to know. I'm sharing this as I wrote it as an honest attempt to strengthen the conviction of a potentially tired or jaded reader who believes in, and works toward bitcoin adoption for similar reasons to myself: freedom from unnecessary human control. I'm not quite sure how to make it less personal, and as this post will reveal, I don't reject all authority as a concept outright. Please be forewarned as, to some, either of those inclusions will certainly be more nauseating than the post if helpful, and I do value your time.

# I got a rejection letter yesterday

It stung so hard. I am pretty sure that I know exactly why I lost this particular opportunity. It was the end of the second interview and the panel asked, "Can you think of a time when you enforced a policy you disagreed with? How did that play out? We're a highly regulated company and we have to enforce many policies involving KYC rules and other legal compliance."

This should have been my clincher moment. I was uncharacteristically nervous though. My phone (despite actually being plugged in) had just died, interrupting the interview for more than a couple of minutes, and I was feeling tense. I reached in my mind for a period of time in which I enforced a policy that I disagreed with.

The following story is **NOT** how I lost my passion for music.

# Covid

In late 2015, after much of my artistic and touring career had been on hold for a few years, I started a branch of a corporate party band company in a midwestern city. I recruited and trained a couple hundred musicians while also booking and managing a few events a month in another established city about two hours away. By the end of the year, I was booking and managing thirty or more events a month in the new city. That following year, I was tasked with bringing order to another neighboring city a few hours away in which the person in my position had been asked to step down. This experience was brutal, as I came in under high suspicion by the musicians, venues, and other vendors alike. For quite a while, everyone there was hostile. Within about a year and a half, that city was doing as well as mine.

When Covid struck, I was supposed to be on my first true, "do-not-contact," vacation in half a decade, yet I spent the first week harshly enforcing contracts, what I still believe was the correct call. This meant that the client was out of a 20% deposit, no small chunk of change, even for the wealthiest people in society. Nevertheless, it's how we protected our musicians, many with families and typically not the wealthiest people in society if they're working the wedding band circuits.

What I shared with my interviewers last week was what started with a phone call in the Denver airport in March of 2020. Despite building their business in a large swath of the midwest, I was instructed by my superiors to enforce **their** new policy about Covid related cancellations.

* First off, we are pausing all cancellation payouts for musicians. I was livid, but there was a silver lining. At least all of these high net worth people that had been yelling at me on the phone the last few days of my "vacation" would get their money and peace of mind back.
* Second off...well you probably already guessed it. We're still keeping the deposits.

So here I am, having made this company millions, enforcing the worst of both worlds. We're keeping the deposits despite the crazy circumstances and breaking our contracts with our contractors, despite our agreements to pay out some fees for cancellations. All this, despite my having built them an operation in the region that had made millions by this point. I made my opinion heard, gritted my teeth while enforcing this policy, and finally trained a few people to replace me after a few months.

# The exact wrong response

So last week I said some platitudes about living in the real world and ended with this depressing tale, portraying myself as a pushover and a quitter. Both of these preparatives are, of course, accurate. But I still think my decisions reflected both my recognition of the proper need for authority and also the integrity to hold the line in the least destructive manner possible. Simply put, my track record trends toward radical, but not for the sake of being radical. I believe last week that I expressed the exact opposite of this in the way I framed this story.

# Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)

Wedding bands are fun. When done right, they're very lucrative. That said, if I never...**ever** hear September, Uptown Funk, Don't Stop Believing, Shake it off, or Crazy in Love again, I'll be just fine. No one ever picked up a guitar with starry-eyed dreams of playing some rich guy's daughter's third wedding. 

But this also is **NOT** how I lost my passion for music.

I actually *really* fell in love with music when I first discovered jazz. Real jazz! Have you ever heard Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Kenny Garrett, John Coltrane, Bill Frisell, Sonny Rollins, Chick Corea, McCoy Tyner, Woody Shaw, Steve Turre, Jaco Pastorious, Curtis Fuller, Pat Metheny, Albert Ayler, Bela Fleck, Courtney Pine, Chris Potter, Eddie Bayard, Paul Brown, Andy Woodson, James Gaiters, Chris Howes, Bobby Floyd, or Derek DiCenzo?! There are so many more. What's even more amazing is that there used to be a pretty strong economy built around this music, and more recently than many here may realize. In the decades before doing the wedding band thing, I spent about half my time performing R\&B (often on the road), but about half my time performing jazz, including with some of my musical heroes listed above.

That economy went away at one point. I had to pivot towards less adventurous musical endeavors. 

But that's also **NOT** how I lost my passion for music.

# How I lost my passion for music

I still love music, and it's how I pay the bills to this day, but you may have gathered already from this post that it's not how I hope to. And I've been trying to make that transition for a while.

A few years back, I was sitting in a club waiting to perform with an "avant garde" jazz ensemble. It paid ostensibly nothing, but there was a really talented "jazz famous" guy sitting in with our group that night and I was kind of excited. The club also gave us all a free burrito and chips. :)

Half way through my chips, some part of my brain heard something that made me pay attention to the conversation at the next table. A member of the band who had a doctorate in "jazz studies" was speaking with our guest artist. He had just been hired by a prestigious university and was describing his curriculum plans. The guest artist made a passing comment about how it sounds like he's institutionalizing jazz music, and the phd guy retorted, "well isn't that the point?"

This was the exact moment that I decided that I want to work in any capacity toward making Bitcoin more successful and accessible. I still enjoy music much more than the average bear, but the sentiment expressed by the phd guy is the exact opposite of what compelled me to tens of thousands of hours of practice back in the day. And it's far from the minority view at this point. Listen to any of my musical heroes listed above and, potentially, the only common thread you'll hear is a lack of institutional rule following. But the youngest of those folks is now the old guard.

It's no coincidence that jazz music originates from, and traditionally thrives in the black community. It is rebel music at it's core. The joy of Louis Armstrong, the complexities of Charlie Parker, and the freedom of Ornette Coleman all establish loose structures (even authority) in an effort to cast aside oppressive control. But "jazz studies" is now a part of normal university curriculum, and despite the standards being way lower than what's necessary to even play cheap bar gigs, the power to codify the rules is established and enforced. I wouldn't go so far as to say, "jazz is dead," but it sure ain't what it used to be...

Furthermore, and more importantly, I found another way to scratch that itch.

# Spoiler Alert (not clickbait)

I'm reading The Two Towers to my two daughters right now. The night after my terminal interview with this bitcoin company, a scene I had long forgot underscored the motivations behind my attempted transitions the last few years and my failure that day at the same time. (last warning, the sentence after next is a huge spoiler) The scene is the forest reunion. Aragorn, Legolas, and Gimli are all reunited with a Gandalf they long thought dead.

As a quick aside, the reunion starts with a mesmerizingly beautiful conversation about Boromir's last day in Middle Earth in which Gandalf is relieved to hear he "escaped." It's a stunning theological lesson about grace, and an example of one of my favorite things about Tolkien's writing. I've long thought that Tolkien is so much more popular with the secular community than his friend C.S. Lewis because all of his preaching goes over all of our heads. Setting aside their essays, and only focusing on the fiction, I'm convinced that Lewis writes philosophy disguised as narrative while Tolkien writes narrative disguised as philosophy. As a result, when reading the former, we bump into offense and sometimes miss a brilliant tale. But when reading the latter, we go on an adventure, and suddenly that amputation on Mount Doom is less than a quarter as exciting (and offensive) as it really should be. I digress.

After confusing the three of them with this speech about Boromir, Gandalf then continues to catch up with another "riddle," to borrow Aragorn's description.

> 'What then shall I say?' said Gandalf, and paused for a while in thought. 'This in brief is how I see things at the moment, if you wish to have a piece of my mind as plain as possible. The Enemy, of course, long has known that the ring is abroad, and that it is borne by a hobbit. He knows now the number of our Company that set out from Rivendell, and the kind of each of us. But he does not yet see our purpose clearly. He supposed that we were all going to Minas Tirith; for that is what he himself would have done in our place. And according to his wisdom it would have been a heavy stroke against his power. Indeed he is in great fear, not knowing what mighty one may suddenly appear, wielding the ring, and assailing his with war, seeking to cast him down and take his place. That we should wish to cast him down and have *no* (emphasis Gandalf's, not mine) one in his place is not a thought that occurs to his mind. That we should try to destroy the ring itself has not yet entered into his darkest dream. In which no doubt you will see our good fortune and our hope. For imagining war he has let lose war, believing that he has no time to waste; for he that strikes the first blow, if he strikes it hard enough, may need to strike no more. So the forces that he has long been preparing he is now setting in motion, sooner than he intended. Wise fool. For if he had used all his power to guard Mordor, so that none could enter, and bent all his guile on the hunting of the Ring, then indeed hope would have faded: neither Ring nor bearer could have long eluded him. But now his eye gazes abroad rather than near at home; and mostly he looks toward Minas Tirith. Very soon now his strength will fall upon it like a storm.'

I have no memory of reading this part as a kid.

I had long remembered the theme throughout this epic that the free peoples of Middle Earth all had to put aside their differences and band together if they wanted to continue their individual ways of life. I've even long enjoyed the funny, annoyed responses Tolkien is recorded giving when people said it was an allegory for either of the world wars since that theme is so similar. But somehow, over the years, I forgot that part of the success of the free people in the Lord of the Rings is the fact that Sauron doesn't even have a **category** for them not wanting someone in charge.

Read that Gandalf quote again and tell me with a straight face that Tolkien wouldn't have been a bitcoiner!

What's wild is that I asked the LLMs about this, and they came up with a totally different passage! "You must be remembering the council of Elrond." Sure enough, I checked and he outlines the same strategy, as well as the enemies same oversight thereof in the first book. I didn't just miss it as a kid, I missed it again when I read it to my girls last month. But it's there, and I think I caught it last Wednesday because of my flub. This is a major theme of the book. Freedom loving people want to minimize human power over others, and the most power-hungry don't even have a category for someone not wanting that power themselves.

# Delegated Authority

I know this is stacker news, and there are a number of folks that I respect here that don't respect those of us that believe authority has a place at all. But I'm in good company. There's no doubt that Tolkien believed in authority. The man was Roman Catholic. Elrond rightly leads the counsel, Gandalf responsibly leads the Fellowship, and ultimately, Aragorn justly leads his country. Yet, he's not as black and white about most moral issues as he's often portrayed. It wasn't enough to keep the ring from Sauron. It wasn't enough to keep the ring from Saruman. It didn't just tempt Boromir. It didn't just take Frodo. The ring was good for **NO MAN**. It's what I loved about jazz. It's what I love about bitcoin. Just like Sauron, the enemies of bitcoin think it's about moving power elsewhere. They have no idea that it might be about removing a whole layer of power altogether. It's why so much of my passion has been sucked into something so seemingly different from what I've spent most of my life doing.

# The response next time

> I believe we need to be radical. But we also need to be effective. Bitcoiners love Hayek's famous, "sly trick" quote, but in practice we are anything but sly when dealing with the uninitiated. I want to do something radical, and I'm convinced this company is doing something radical. I want to see a more fair, just, and prospering world, but I don't think we get there with chaos. I believe in freedom **and** authority. When authority is abused, I don't jump to chaos as a response, but I want to fight alongside and for people that reject needless control. Now that we have bitcoin, needless control is what the dollar has become. I would like to be with an organization that is working towards dissolving that control.

# The cross comes before the crown and tomorrow is a Monday morning!

The above quote is from Tolkien's friend C.S. Lewis. He's talking about even loftier ideas in the essay quoted (The Weight of Glory), but the point applies to this work as well. The past seven months have been pretty depressing for me. After going whole hog on trying to setup a bitcoin project last year, I'm back to playing local gigs. Sometimes it's so joyful. That's what the best music always is. Sometimes it's work. That's good too. But a lot of what I've worked so hard for has been consumed pursuing "bitcoin stuff." Maybe you've had setbacks too. If you have, I hope you remember what's so exciting about the opportunity this technology presents. If bitcoin succeeds in the manner that many on this forum hope it will:

**No one will be in control of the money.**

That's not just a clever approach that breaks the rules. That's something that will change people's lives. Maybe I won't ever get my bitcoin job. There are plenty of ways outside of a job to pursue this end. There are also other noble pursuits (some greater) which we should pursue as well. But that's a darn good one.

items.title: A thousand people can own one Bitcoin transaction.
items.text:
> Ark gets pitched as "the next Lightning." It solves a similar problem — instant, cheap, self-custodial Bitcoin payments — with an almost opposite design. Understanding the difference tells you what each one is actually for.


## They solve the same problem two almost-opposite ways.

It's natural to reach for Lightning as the comparison — it's the only other Bitcoin layer running at real scale. But the mechanics share very little. Lightning routes a payment across a chain of bilateral channels; every hop needs its own pre-funded, balanced liquidity, and receiving means either staying online or paying a service to watch for you. Ark has no routing graph at all — a payment simply swaps a share of one pooled output for a share of a new one, cosigned by the ASP, done.

![](https://m.stacker.news/152783)

The two aren't strictly rivals, either. ASPs commonly run a Lightning gateway, letting Ark users send and receive real Lightning payments without operating a Lightning node of their own. And in July 2026, Lightning Labs — the company behind Lightning's most widely used implementation — released an early, Ark-like settlement layer of its own, aimed at agent-to-agent payments. Even the Lightning side sees a use for shared-UTXO batching.

items.title: Speculating about bitcoin-standard wages
items.text:
@denlillaapan raised a perpetually interesting question in [his post](https://stacker.news/items/1552045/r/Undisciplined) earlier today: How can wages be sustainable for employers on a sound money standard?

The problem is simple enough. If the money is appreciating, then the nominal wage rate will keep getting more expensive for the employer and workers get real prickly about taking pay cuts (hello sticky wages).

# **Natural Real Raises**

Let's start with the simplest case, where the nominal wage is maintained. For the employee, the appreciating currency serves as a natural pay raise. The same nominal pay buys more stuff over time. For the employer, each employee becomes more expensive over time.

If the rate of appreciation is modest, this might work well enough. People get better at their jobs with more experience and typically receive raises and promotions, anyway, so they would likely justify the added real expense (especially if they're assuming more responsibilities with seniority).

What would change in this setting is starting pay. New workers would be offered lower nominal wages than experienced workers.

# **Term Contracts**

If monetary appreciation is greater than productivity gains from experience, employers will have to find ways to reduce nominal pay over time. Let's assume away the boring case where workers just get used to the idea of falling wages.

One easy option is something we see in sports: term contracts. Maybe it will become normal to sign an employee to a three year deal at a particular wage, with an understanding that the terms will have to be renegotiated.

The employer will have a better idea of their financial situation towards the end of the term, as well as the employees productivity, and they can make an extension offer. The employee will also have a clearer picture of their outside options, which will help both sides converge to something like the right real rate of pay.

In cases of rapid monetary appreciation, employers could also negotiate lower pay on the current contract in exchange for a longer guaranteed contract. This is very common in the NFL, for instance (not because of an appreciating currency, tho).

# **Profit Sharing**

My go-to answer for this question has generally been profit sharing arrangements. These would likely be hybrid contracts, with a base salary and an equity share of some sort.

There are several nice features of contracts like this:

* Incentive alignment: employees benefit more as the company does better
* The equity portion is self-correcting: the company's nominal labor expenses vary with its ability to pay.
* If the base salary is small, even high rates of monetary appreciation might be compensated for by human capital gains to productivity.

The downside here is largely that employees don't generally want to internalize the financial risks of a business, preferring instead a steady rate of pay at a lower average level. In this model, it would be the new employees relying more heavily on the equity share of their compensation, while being the least able to absorb the fluctuations.

# **Independent Contracting**

The other option is that the work model we've become so accustomed to will breakdown almost entirely and most people will become independent contractors. This would require the coordination frictions that firms solve to be overcome by the productivity gains from the improved incentives of independent contracting (I find this far-fetched).

In this world, we wouldn't have bosses and employers. We would have customers and clients. There would be frequent revisions to compensation rates, as new terms are negotiate with each job, and people would experience relatively large fluctuations in pay. 

I strongly doubt that most people have any interest in this situation and would accept significantly lower pay to avoid it.

***

My guess is that all of the above will play a role, should we make meaningful progress towards a bitcoin standard.

What do you think we'll see?

items.title: Don't switch your Core Lightning node off, restart it with --offline instead
items.text:
Core Lightning has been triaging a high volume of AI-generated CVE reports over recent weeks. Several are real, and a coordinated fix is underway.

What to do now: do not shut your node down. Restart it with --offline.

That flag stops peer connections, so no payments route in, out or through your node. It keeps running, which means it keeps watching the chain and can still act if a counterparty force-closes a channel. A node that is powered off cannot do that, and that is why switching off is the worse option.

On @umbrel or @start9labs this is a startup setting for Core Lightning, not a toggle in the dashboard.

What happens next: signed binaries will be published. Verify the signatures before you install, then bring your node back online. Source and reproducible builds follow afterwards so anyone can audit what changed.

items.title: BIP SHRINCS (draft)
items.text:
The work on post quantum signatures for Bitcoin continues to advance. Here we have a formal BIP draft for SHRINCS (*SPHINCS*), a hash-based post-quantum signature scheme):

> SHRINCS offers compact post-quantum signatures under conservative cryptographic assumptions. It relies solely on the security of its underlying hash function. In this specification, that function is SHA256, which is already fundamental to Bitcoin's security. Signature schemes from other post-quantum families also rely on hash-function security but additionally require separate hardness assumptions, such as the hardness of lattice problems. Bitcoin outputs may remain unspent for long periods, making conservative cryptographic assumptions particularly valuable. This conservatism gives hash-based signature schemes like SHRINCS a distinct place in the cryptographic design space, even when schemes from other families offer better size or performance.
>  
> Signature size is particularly important in Bitcoin because signatures consume scarce block space. SHRINCS therefore offers signers a compact stateful signing path at the cost of additional implementation complexity. This path allows SHRINCS to leverage the fact that a key pair in Bitcoin is typically used only a few times. As a result, stateful SHRINCS signatures can be many times smaller than those of standardized hash-based signature schemes. The minimum combined size of a SHRINCS public key and stateful signature is roughly 13.23x smaller than that of SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s[<sup>2</sup>](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/SHRINCS.md#user-content-fn-slhdsa-5265daea9ed2eac499a3e955656e322e) and 6.26x smaller than that of the lattice-based ML-DSA-44 scheme (which targets NIST security category 2, whereas SHRINCS targets category 1).

There's also a Bitcoin developers mailing lost post: https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev/c/HbVboXIFiG8

Have a look at the draft if you find this kind of stuff interesting, and don't let anyone tell you that bitcoiners aren't taking quantum seriously.

On the Economics of Inflation-Protected Securities
items.text:
Nobody [but a blockhead](https://www.brainyquote.com/quotes/samuel_johnson_170103) (=economist) likes indexation.

I mentioned this phenomenon in passing last week (https://stacker.news/items/1552045) — e.g., [Shiller’s paper](https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/1997/01/1997a_bpea_shiller_schultze_hall.pdf) from 1997 — but meant to delve into it more thoroughly.

Here’s my summary of the distributional concerns from the Economics of Peer-to-Peer post:

***

> ## **The Puzzle of the Public's Dislike of Indexation**

> The opposition to indexation has long puzzled economists, i.e., those of us with odd minds that think about money, money illusion, and the (un)fairness of nominal contracts/payments when the real worth of money changes. To recap the deep, long, important economic intellectual convo:

* if I make a loan to you at $100 for one year and at 5% interest, but at the end of the year the price level is 10% higher, *I lost out 5% while loaning you funds*.
* If I make a loan to you at $100 for one year and at 5% interest, but at the end of the year the price level is 2% higher, the real rate of interest was only 3%.

> There are a couple of ways that banks (and more sophisticated securities markets and futures contracts) could deal with this, where the most common one is for the bank to have in-house experts forecasting the future price level and price loans accordingly. That is, if they're willing to lend to you at 3% and they *believe* the Fed will hit 2%, the loan contract will say 5% -- hashtag all the way back to Irving Fisher, and in honest to every merchant and money-lender throughout history.

> The *other*, more obvious, option would be to **just adjust the principal (= the $100) by the inflation rate after the fact, leaving the (real) interest rate intact.** So in the first scenario, the loan balance due (without repayments) would be $115 after one year -- $5 interest, $10 adjustment -- and in the second scenario, the loan balance would be $107.

***

Basically, it’s an old and longstanding theoretical consideration of *who*, *precisely* [bear the burden of money’s shifting worth](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/who-bears-the-burden-of-dollars-falling-purchasing-power/).

Here’s Shiller again, saying not quite hyperbolically that this resistance to indexation is “one of the greatest economic puzzles of all time”:

> That the public should generally want to denominate contracts in currency units —despite all the evidence that **it is not wise to do so and despite the obvious examples from nominal contracts of redistributions caused by unexpected inflation** — should be regarded as one of the great economic puzzles of all time.

## “The success of the U.S. Treasury’s first issuance of consumer price-indexed debt in January 1997 does virtually nothing to diminish the salience of this puzzle”

Ergo Satoshi quote ([Letters 10:15](https://canon.satsdisco.com/#/letters/10/16)).

In the meantime, we have Jason Zweig, a longtime WSJ columnist on matters of personal finance who has quite frequently invoked TIPS — the U.S. Treasury’s own indexed bonds. They have notoriously (shockingly) low uptake despite being, as Zweig wrote in the *Wall Street Journal* yesterday, **“the closest thing to a risk-free investment.”**

Or, at least, *somewhat* risk-free:

> Fellow investors,
> You might spend some of a staycation playing golf, camping or binge-watching your favorite TV show. I spent some of mine buying inflation-protected bonds.

Hashtag lol. Continuing the madness:

> Last week, I sat on the screen porch with an iced tea and put a substantial part of my IRA into TIPS at real yields of up to 3%. (I didn’t buy a TIPS ETF or mutual fund; I bought individual TIPS on the secondary market, in my brokerage account.)
> you can lock in today’s historically generous rates if, *but only if,* you buy individual TIPS (not a TIPS fund) and hold them to maturity.

All the trust involved for this supposedly “risk-free” investment is the (admittedly quite low) risk of Treasury not paying you, but more importantly the risk that the actual-real value — i.e., what future money *gets* you — will fall well short of the 3% real Zweig envisions.

It’s not, as many Bitcoiners uncritically suppose, that the U.S. agency for calculating the inflation rate (= statisticians at the Bureau of Labor Statistics) are crooks, beholden to the President, or systematically biasing the rates to be lower than *akschual* real-world inflation. It’s that constructing an average price index is backward-looking, impossible, and a hopeless endeavor: how much better is "communication" or "light" today vs 20, 200, or 2000 years ago? Hedonic adjustments shove it downwards; quality improvements upward; "free" stuff (think YouTube) makes the basket lower than it would have been.  

Zweig goes on to remark on the fiscal troubles facing America’s government (yes, we know: https://stacker.news/items/1554544 https://stacker.news/items/1554571, https://stacker.news/items/1554591)

> What makes me feel bad is that “the closest thing to a risk-free investment” isn’t as close as it used to be. The gross U.S. debt [surpassed $40 trillion earlier this month](https:/www.wsj.com/economy/u-s-debt-just-topped-40-trillion-how-we-got-here-c1c6c9d2)—approaching its highest level, as a percentage of GDP, since shortly after World War II. Net interest payments, which consumed only 1.3% of GDP in 2016, totaled 3.2% of GDP in 2025. And, with [bond yields at their highest in nearly two decades](https:/www.wsj.com/finance/investing/bonds-are-getting-hammered-and-wall-street-says-the-rout-wont-end-anytime-soon-895e0ad8), that interest burden is almost sure to balloon.

What I like about indexation products -- at least on the *savings* side because that's where I hang out, not having a mortgage because, you know, ownership obsession [https://www.stacker.news/items/1459569](https://www.stacker.news/items/1459569) -- is that the unanticipated surprise inflation (biased as it is, on the upside) protects me.

Standard savings account earn 7% (remember, these lands and their incompetent monetary rulers run structurally higher inflation and rates: https://stacker.news/items/1555171 -- 10y yield is 6.9%, IOR 8%). My indexed savings account yield 2% (not unlike Zweig's TIPS, btw), *plus* whatever the statistics agency says the inflation is.

* If inflation undershoots, i.e. 4%, I am roughly OK (2% interest + 4% adjustment for a \~6% nominal gain) but relatively speaking lose -- could have earned 7% on a regular savings account.
* If inflation overshoots, i.e., 6%, I am *also* roughly OK (2% interest + 6% adjustment for a \~8% nominal gain -- but I relatively gain, since regular savings account would have paid me only 7%.

Plus, it \_does\_ feel pretty cool when my "principal" (= savings account amount) adjusts in hindsight depending on what happened to the inflation reading \_rather\_ than the predicted/previously stated interest rate. 

Since I think there's more than even odds for the monetary clown hats https://stacker.news/items/747181 to *overshoot*, **I rather keep slightly more fiat for immediate bills in the indexed products than the standard savings account.**

Of course, these products don't "earn" you anything; can't *save* your way into wealth or improve your financial standing in any material way. It's keeping you afloat, preventing you from immediately drowning. Wealth, and wealth generation, comes from riding the fiat wave on hard assets -- bitcoin, gold, stocks, and yes houses (with short fiat, e.g., debt https://stacker.news/items/994746); so full circle.

## Anyway, I like indexation. I think the future of Bitcoinland includes more of it

items.title: Dear citizens of the universe and beyond
items.text:
Hello,

I come to you from a small blue planet called Earth to share my experiences with a groundbreaking substance known as kefir.

I am beyond appalled by its wonders. (Okay, I wanted to continue this as if I were some kind of alien, but I kept grinning and one of my cats started screaming at the other, so the fantasy kinda broke. Now they’re play-fighting and doing cat stuff like ignoring each other all of a sudden).

Anyway let me tell you about kefir. 

Even though I briefly had some milk kefir at home a few years ago, we had to part ways. It wasn’t until about a month ago that I bought dry kefir grains and activated them, in the middle of a heat wave, mind you! They’ve been doing great.

They haven’t grown that much yet. I’ve read that, supposedly, dry grains don’t grow as much, and in the beginning, with the heat wave and their first cycles, they’re more interested in stabilizing themselves than actually growing. But oh boy, they’ve been giving me a cup of kefir a day.

During the heat wave, it was more like two cups a day :D. It was intense. Now they’ve slowed down and grown just a bit, but they’re getting there.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/a40c5d48-0c24-4169-896d-177e95fc60b8_img_8720.jpeg)Those kefir grains were working overtime 

They have that tangy taste, though it wasn’t like that at first, it was sour and tasted so acidic. It wasn’t until maybe 7 or 8 cycles that I changed the milk that they started to show larger and actually produce something more similar to kefir. I was getting worried though, I thought they were not gonna make it. 

This photo was taken just six days after I first started activating the grains. Before this, they were so small I could barely distinguish them in the milk.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/29187b7a-4ab1-4094-a3e5-5774309522fa_img_8701.jpeg)

In my experience, if kefir separates, it’s because it’s been sitting way too long with the same milk and needs to be changed. It smells even more fermented than usual, but you only have to swirl it a bit and leave it in the fridge for a few hours, and you’re good to go.

The hotter it is, the quicker it ferments, so watch out—maybe in less than 12 hours the milk needs to be changed again.

I've been enjoying kefir so much and with it I've been making strawberry smoothies ⬇️ 

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/6e409ec2-e8e8-451b-9bcf-762f7bc3a49e_img_8721.jpeg)She says that's not chicken soup ![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/658718a1-d8b9-4d5b-a9c8-10c46f5564db_img_8728.jpeg)Peach and kefir smoothie 

And I've also been having it on its own.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/5efbe02d-67eb-46e8-a718-195b40fa33d0_img_8735.jpeg)Look at all those bubbles 😌

It’s true, this one doesn’t taste like the one at the grocery store. Mine is a bit “watery” because it doesn’t take "that long" to ferment (and it's not that cold but not that hot either), but it tastes tangy and smells like milk fermentation. So, I'm set. 

Sometimes, even before you taste it, you’ll get that smell and be 99.9% sure it’s done. Once you taste it, you get that final 0.1%.

I guess my point is: it is worth it. It took me a while, but oh wow, it is so much better than store-bought. And you basically have it for life if it’s properly taken care of. Another benefit from kefir, if you ask me. 

Would you get kefir and ferment it at home, or is it too much hassle for what it’s worth to you? I’d like to know, hehehe.

In the meantime, don’t worry, righteous citizens of this Earth. I’m working on a [new blog entry ](https://samhainsam.art/blog/)*rubs hands*. As usual, I’m quite excited, so sit tight, it will be worth it, hehehehe.

See you later, alligator 🐊

PS I've baked some brownie cookies, some tiramisu and some gooey chocolate chips cookies (not pictured) Yay!

items.title: Testing out Gridpool.net
items.text:
Check out gridpool.net

I'm testing it out right now, just for fun but also looking for new mining projects for my itty bitty fleet.  This is a different payout scheme idea where the payout goes to the workers that have submitted the highest difficulty work ; so the miners do not necessarily need to be actively submitting work to receive the payout if the pool were to find a valid block and have it accepted by the network.  Cool visual graphic too for the workflow: [https://main.gridpool.net/](https://main.gridpool.net/)

![](https://m.stacker.news/153760)

I am currently sending work from a bitaxe to test it out.  I have the bitaxe running via DATUM on my start9.  Gridpool has instructions for how to update your DATUM config to point to their pool.  It was very easy, simply copy/pasting a few lines.  Watched it accept a few shares seems to all be working.

![](https://m.stacker.news/153759)

The project has some ambitious ideas to be able to have separate gridpool operators Federate, seems like it would be something akin to p2pool.

Pod256 had the creator of gridpool on their show recently: [https://www.pod256.org/episodepage/116-decentralizing-pool-payouts-inside-gridpool-with-agent-p](https://www.pod256.org/episodepage/116-decentralizing-pool-payouts-inside-gridpool-with-agent-p)

items.title: French Top Court Gets It Right, Strikes Down Social Media Ban For Youths
items.text:
winning https://stacker.news/items/650239/r/k00b?commentId=650288

> Earlier this month, France’s top court [struck down](https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/actualites/communique/decision-n-2026-911-dc-du-14-aout-2026-communique-de-presse) the country’s legislation that [banned social media](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq56l9p4y93o) use for people under 15 years old, which had been scheduled to take effect in January 2027. This is a welcome win for free expression, as we face a wave of [countries and U.S. states](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/how-and-why-fight-back-against-social-media-bans) seeking to pass similar laws banning young people from social media.

> The Council [ruled](https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/actualites/communique/decision-n-2026-911-dc-du-14-aout-2026-communique-de-presse) that the legislation banning under-15s from social media infringed on freedom of expression and communication in a manner that is not appropriate, necessary, or proportionate, which is required by Article 34 of the French Constitution. In particular, it stressed that the ban did not distinguish between different types of online services, and ignored the circumstances of individual users, such as their exact age, level of maturity, and family situation.

> The French Council gets a lot right in this decision: it highlights that bans like this impact not just young people, but everyone online. They force people of all ages to hand over [government IDs](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/12/why-isnt-online-age-verification-just-showing-your-id-person), [face scans](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/01/face-scans-estimate-our-age-creepy-af-and-harmful), and [other sensitive information](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/lgbt-qa-what-data-are-companies-uk-collecting-when-verifying-my-age) into a growing surveillance ecosystem. Further, when parental consent is required, companies must collect [even more](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/05/law-should-not-require-parental-consent-all-minors-access-social-media) verification data on the parents.

items.title: Don't switch your Core Lightning node off, restart it with --offline instead
items.text:
Core Lightning has been triaging a high volume of AI-generated CVE reports over recent weeks. Several are real, and a coordinated fix is underway.

What to do now: do not shut your node down. Restart it with --offline.

That flag stops peer connections, so no payments route in, out or through your node. It keeps running, which means it keeps watching the chain and can still act if a counterparty force-closes a channel. A node that is powered off cannot do that, and that is why switching off is the worse option.

On @umbrel or @start9labs this is a startup setting for Core Lightning, not a toggle in the dashboard.

What happens next: signed binaries will be published. Verify the signatures before you install, then bring your node back online. Source and reproducible builds follow afterwards so anyone can audit what changed.

http://github.com/ElementsProject/lightning

> At that same event, her deputy praised the government's blockchain-tracing partner, Chainalysis.
>  
> Here is what they didn't tell the audience. All of it is from the public docket in my case.
>  
> According to the trial transcripts, Chainalysis was running its OWN Tornado Cash relayer, and earning fees on the transactions flowing through it.
>  
> - Chainalysis's own lawyers admitted to "a relayer node that Chainalysis operated"; my subpoena sought documents on Tornado Cash relayer(s) "used from March to August 2022." (Dkt. 211)
> - In open court, the prosecutor said it plainly: "I think the parties agree as to that part of the testimony, that the Chainalysis relayer earned fees." Same hearing: "there's zero evidence that the defendant was in any way aware that Chainalysis was running a relayer." (Dkt. 259, July 25, 2025)
>  
> So the company that helped trace my "criminal" transactions was itself profiting from Tornado Cash transactions, while I was prosecuted over software I helped create.
>  
> And when my lawyers subpoenaed them to testify?
>  
> - Chainalysis moved to quash. (Dkt. 211)
> - The government backed them: "Your Honor, we agree with the position outlined in the motion." (Dkt. 255)
> - The night before, prosecutors called Chainalysis's counsel. The judge asked point-blank: "Did you let them know that they were potentially subject to investigation or prosecution?" The answer: "We have discussed at a high level some of the issues surrounding the relayer with Chainalysis." (Dkt. 259)
> - The Chainalysis witness took the Fifth. My lawyers learned about that call only afterward, from Chainalysis's own lawyer. (Dkt. 263)
>  
> The jury never heard any of it.
>  
> This spring, at the Bitcoin 2026 conference in Las Vegas, something happened that I still can't quite believe. The Acting Attorney General, Todd Blanche, and the FBI Director, Kash Patel, sat on a panel called "Code is Free Speech."
>  
> Think about that. The two top law enforcement officials in the country. Blanche told thousands of developers: if you're a coder and you're not the one committing the crime, "you are not going to be investigated and not going to be charged." He said the last administration's crypto cases were "outrageous attacks on the industry." Patel praised "the Chainalysises of the world" as FBI partners.
>  
> And when the moderator pointed at the elephant in the room, my case, Tornado Cash, Roman Storm, the Acting Attorney General called it a "lingering case" they are "continuing to deal with."
>  
> So here is my hypothetical question. If code is free speech, why am I still being prosecuted for writing it? And if the Chainalysises of the world are the partners, the same Chainalysis that ran its own Tornado Cash relayer and earned fees from Tornado Cash users, while I never did, why is it off the hook?
>  
> They made an example out of a developer for writing code. Their own vendor ran the same infrastructure, pocketed the fees, and got a phone call instead of a prosecution.

I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

items.title: BIP SHRINCS (draft)
items.text:
The work on post quantum signatures for Bitcoin continues to advance. Here we have a formal BIP draft for SHRINCS (*SPHINCS*), a hash-based post-quantum signature scheme):

> SHRINCS offers compact post-quantum signatures under conservative cryptographic assumptions. It relies solely on the security of its underlying hash function. In this specification, that function is SHA256, which is already fundamental to Bitcoin's security. Signature schemes from other post-quantum families also rely on hash-function security but additionally require separate hardness assumptions, such as the hardness of lattice problems. Bitcoin outputs may remain unspent for long periods, making conservative cryptographic assumptions particularly valuable. This conservatism gives hash-based signature schemes like SHRINCS a distinct place in the cryptographic design space, even when schemes from other families offer better size or performance.
>  
> Signature size is particularly important in Bitcoin because signatures consume scarce block space. SHRINCS therefore offers signers a compact stateful signing path at the cost of additional implementation complexity. This path allows SHRINCS to leverage the fact that a key pair in Bitcoin is typically used only a few times. As a result, stateful SHRINCS signatures can be many times smaller than those of standardized hash-based signature schemes. The minimum combined size of a SHRINCS public key and stateful signature is roughly 13.23x smaller than that of SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s[<sup>2</sup>](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/SHRINCS.md#user-content-fn-slhdsa-5265daea9ed2eac499a3e955656e322e) and 6.26x smaller than that of the lattice-based ML-DSA-44 scheme (which targets NIST security category 2, whereas SHRINCS targets category 1).

There's also a Bitcoin developers mailing lost post: https://groups.google.com/g/bitcoindev/c/HbVboXIFiG8

Have a look at the draft if you find this kind of stuff interesting, and don't let anyone tell you that bitcoiners aren't taking quantum seriously.

On the Economics of Inflation-Protected Securities
items.text:
Nobody [but a blockhead](https://www.brainyquote.com/quotes/samuel_johnson_170103) (=economist) likes indexation.

I mentioned this phenomenon in passing last week (https://stacker.news/items/1552045) — e.g., [Shiller’s paper](https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/1997/01/1997a_bpea_shiller_schultze_hall.pdf) from 1997 — but meant to delve into it more thoroughly.

Here’s my summary of the distributional concerns from the Economics of Peer-to-Peer post:

***

> ## **The Puzzle of the Public's Dislike of Indexation**

> The opposition to indexation has long puzzled economists, i.e., those of us with odd minds that think about money, money illusion, and the (un)fairness of nominal contracts/payments when the real worth of money changes. To recap the deep, long, important economic intellectual convo:

* if I make a loan to you at $100 for one year and at 5% interest, but at the end of the year the price level is 10% higher, *I lost out 5% while loaning you funds*.
* If I make a loan to you at $100 for one year and at 5% interest, but at the end of the year the price level is 2% higher, the real rate of interest was only 3%.

> There are a couple of ways that banks (and more sophisticated securities markets and futures contracts) could deal with this, where the most common one is for the bank to have in-house experts forecasting the future price level and price loans accordingly. That is, if they're willing to lend to you at 3% and they *believe* the Fed will hit 2%, the loan contract will say 5% -- hashtag all the way back to Irving Fisher, and in honest to every merchant and money-lender throughout history.

> The *other*, more obvious, option would be to **just adjust the principal (= the $100) by the inflation rate after the fact, leaving the (real) interest rate intact.** So in the first scenario, the loan balance due (without repayments) would be $115 after one year -- $5 interest, $10 adjustment -- and in the second scenario, the loan balance would be $107.

***

Basically, it’s an old and longstanding theoretical consideration of *who*, *precisely* [bear the burden of money’s shifting worth](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/who-bears-the-burden-of-dollars-falling-purchasing-power/).

Here’s Shiller again, saying not quite hyperbolically that this resistance to indexation is “one of the greatest economic puzzles of all time”:

> That the public should generally want to denominate contracts in currency units —despite all the evidence that **it is not wise to do so and despite the obvious examples from nominal contracts of redistributions caused by unexpected inflation** — should be regarded as one of the great economic puzzles of all time.

## “The success of the U.S. Treasury’s first issuance of consumer price-indexed debt in January 1997 does virtually nothing to diminish the salience of this puzzle”

Ergo Satoshi quote ([Letters 10:15](https://canon.satsdisco.com/#/letters/10/16)).

In the meantime, we have Jason Zweig, a longtime WSJ columnist on matters of personal finance who has quite frequently invoked TIPS — the U.S. Treasury’s own indexed bonds. They have notoriously (shockingly) low uptake despite being, as Zweig wrote in the *Wall Street Journal* yesterday, **“the closest thing to a risk-free investment.”**

Or, at least, *somewhat* risk-free:

> Fellow investors,
> You might spend some of a staycation playing golf, camping or binge-watching your favorite TV show. I spent some of mine buying inflation-protected bonds.

Hashtag lol. Continuing the madness:

> Last week, I sat on the screen porch with an iced tea and put a substantial part of my IRA into TIPS at real yields of up to 3%. (I didn’t buy a TIPS ETF or mutual fund; I bought individual TIPS on the secondary market, in my brokerage account.)
> you can lock in today’s historically generous rates if, *but only if,* you buy individual TIPS (not a TIPS fund) and hold them to maturity.

All the trust involved for this supposedly “risk-free” investment is the (admittedly quite low) risk of Treasury not paying you, but more importantly the risk that the actual-real value — i.e., what future money *gets* you — will fall well short of the 3% real Zweig envisions.

It’s not, as many Bitcoiners uncritically suppose, that the U.S. agency for calculating the inflation rate (= statisticians at the Bureau of Labor Statistics) are crooks, beholden to the President, or systematically biasing the rates to be lower than *akschual* real-world inflation. It’s that constructing an average price index is backward-looking, impossible, and a hopeless endeavor: how much better is "communication" or "light" today vs 20, 200, or 2000 years ago? Hedonic adjustments shove it downwards; quality improvements upward; "free" stuff (think YouTube) makes the basket lower than it would have been.  

Zweig goes on to remark on the fiscal troubles facing America’s government (yes, we know: https://stacker.news/items/1554544 https://stacker.news/items/1554571, https://stacker.news/items/1554591)

> What makes me feel bad is that “the closest thing to a risk-free investment” isn’t as close as it used to be. The gross U.S. debt [surpassed $40 trillion earlier this month](https:/www.wsj.com/economy/u-s-debt-just-topped-40-trillion-how-we-got-here-c1c6c9d2)—approaching its highest level, as a percentage of GDP, since shortly after World War II. Net interest payments, which consumed only 1.3% of GDP in 2016, totaled 3.2% of GDP in 2025. And, with [bond yields at their highest in nearly two decades](https:/www.wsj.com/finance/investing/bonds-are-getting-hammered-and-wall-street-says-the-rout-wont-end-anytime-soon-895e0ad8), that interest burden is almost sure to balloon.

What I like about indexation products -- at least on the *savings* side because that's where I hang out, not having a mortgage because, you know, ownership obsession [https://www.stacker.news/items/1459569](https://www.stacker.news/items/1459569) -- is that the unanticipated surprise inflation (biased as it is, on the upside) protects me.

Standard savings account earn 7% (remember, these lands and their incompetent monetary rulers run structurally higher inflation and rates: https://stacker.news/items/1555171 -- 10y yield is 6.9%, IOR 8%). My indexed savings account yield 2% (not unlike Zweig's TIPS, btw), *plus* whatever the statistics agency says the inflation is.

* If inflation undershoots, i.e. 4%, I am roughly OK (2% interest + 4% adjustment for a \~6% nominal gain) but relatively speaking lose -- could have earned 7% on a regular savings account.
* If inflation overshoots, i.e., 6%, I am *also* roughly OK (2% interest + 6% adjustment for a \~8% nominal gain -- but I relatively gain, since regular savings account would have paid me only 7%.

Plus, it \_does\_ feel pretty cool when my "principal" (= savings account amount) adjusts in hindsight depending on what happened to the inflation reading \_rather\_ than the predicted/previously stated interest rate. 

Since I think there's more than even odds for the monetary clown hats https://stacker.news/items/747181 to *overshoot*, **I rather keep slightly more fiat for immediate bills in the indexed products than the standard savings account.**

Of course, these products don't "earn" you anything; can't *save* your way into wealth or improve your financial standing in any material way. It's keeping you afloat, preventing you from immediately drowning. Wealth, and wealth generation, comes from riding the fiat wave on hard assets -- bitcoin, gold, stocks, and yes houses (with short fiat, e.g., debt https://stacker.news/items/994746); so full circle.

## Anyway, I like indexation. I think the future of Bitcoinland includes more of it

items.title: Dear citizens of the universe and beyond
items.text:
Hello,

I come to you from a small blue planet called Earth to share my experiences with a groundbreaking substance known as kefir.

I am beyond appalled by its wonders. (Okay, I wanted to continue this as if I were some kind of alien, but I kept grinning and one of my cats started screaming at the other, so the fantasy kinda broke. Now they’re play-fighting and doing cat stuff like ignoring each other all of a sudden).

Anyway let me tell you about kefir. 

Even though I briefly had some milk kefir at home a few years ago, we had to part ways. It wasn’t until about a month ago that I bought dry kefir grains and activated them, in the middle of a heat wave, mind you! They’ve been doing great.

They haven’t grown that much yet. I’ve read that, supposedly, dry grains don’t grow as much, and in the beginning, with the heat wave and their first cycles, they’re more interested in stabilizing themselves than actually growing. But oh boy, they’ve been giving me a cup of kefir a day.

During the heat wave, it was more like two cups a day :D. It was intense. Now they’ve slowed down and grown just a bit, but they’re getting there.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/a40c5d48-0c24-4169-896d-177e95fc60b8_img_8720.jpeg)Those kefir grains were working overtime 

They have that tangy taste, though it wasn’t like that at first, it was sour and tasted so acidic. It wasn’t until maybe 7 or 8 cycles that I changed the milk that they started to show larger and actually produce something more similar to kefir. I was getting worried though, I thought they were not gonna make it. 

This photo was taken just six days after I first started activating the grains. Before this, they were so small I could barely distinguish them in the milk.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/29187b7a-4ab1-4094-a3e5-5774309522fa_img_8701.jpeg)

In my experience, if kefir separates, it’s because it’s been sitting way too long with the same milk and needs to be changed. It smells even more fermented than usual, but you only have to swirl it a bit and leave it in the fridge for a few hours, and you’re good to go.

The hotter it is, the quicker it ferments, so watch out—maybe in less than 12 hours the milk needs to be changed again.

I've been enjoying kefir so much and with it I've been making strawberry smoothies ⬇️ 

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/6e409ec2-e8e8-451b-9bcf-762f7bc3a49e_img_8721.jpeg)She says that's not chicken soup ![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/658718a1-d8b9-4d5b-a9c8-10c46f5564db_img_8728.jpeg)Peach and kefir smoothie 

And I've also been having it on its own.

![](https://storage.ko-fi.com/cdn/useruploads/display/5efbe02d-67eb-46e8-a718-195b40fa33d0_img_8735.jpeg)Look at all those bubbles 😌

It’s true, this one doesn’t taste like the one at the grocery store. Mine is a bit “watery” because it doesn’t take "that long" to ferment (and it's not that cold but not that hot either), but it tastes tangy and smells like milk fermentation. So, I'm set. 

Sometimes, even before you taste it, you’ll get that smell and be 99.9% sure it’s done. Once you taste it, you get that final 0.1%.

I guess my point is: it is worth it. It took me a while, but oh wow, it is so much better than store-bought. And you basically have it for life if it’s properly taken care of. Another benefit from kefir, if you ask me. 

Would you get kefir and ferment it at home, or is it too much hassle for what it’s worth to you? I’d like to know, hehehe.

In the meantime, don’t worry, righteous citizens of this Earth. I’m working on a [new blog entry ](https://samhainsam.art/blog/)*rubs hands*. As usual, I’m quite excited, so sit tight, it will be worth it, hehehehe.

See you later, alligator 🐊

PS I've baked some brownie cookies, some tiramisu and some gooey chocolate chips cookies (not pictured) Yay!

Check out gridpool.net

I'm testing it out right now, just for fun but also looking for new mining projects for my itty bitty fleet.  This is a different payout scheme idea where the payout goes to the workers that have submitted the highest difficulty work ; so the miners do not necessarily need to be actively submitting work to receive the payout if the pool were to find a valid block and have it accepted by the network.  Cool visual graphic too for the workflow: [https://main.gridpool.net/](https://main.gridpool.net/)

![](https://m.stacker.news/153760)

I am currently sending work from a bitaxe to test it out.  I have the bitaxe running via DATUM on my start9.  Gridpool has instructions for how to update your DATUM config to point to their pool.  It was very easy, simply copy/pasting a few lines.  Watched it accept a few shares seems to all be working.

![](https://m.stacker.news/153759)

The project has some ambitious ideas to be able to have separate gridpool operators Federate, seems like it would be something akin to p2pool.

items.title: French Top Court Gets It Right, Strikes Down Social Media Ban For Youths
items.text:
winning https://stacker.news/items/650239/r/k00b?commentId=650288

> Earlier this month, France’s top court [struck down](https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/actualites/communique/decision-n-2026-911-dc-du-14-aout-2026-communique-de-presse) the country’s legislation that [banned social media](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq56l9p4y93o) use for people under 15 years old, which had been scheduled to take effect in January 2027. This is a welcome win for free expression, as we face a wave of [countries and U.S. states](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/how-and-why-fight-back-against-social-media-bans) seeking to pass similar laws banning young people from social media.

> The Council [ruled](https://www.conseil-constitutionnel.fr/actualites/communique/decision-n-2026-911-dc-du-14-aout-2026-communique-de-presse) that the legislation banning under-15s from social media infringed on freedom of expression and communication in a manner that is not appropriate, necessary, or proportionate, which is required by Article 34 of the French Constitution. In particular, it stressed that the ban did not distinguish between different types of online services, and ignored the circumstances of individual users, such as their exact age, level of maturity, and family situation.

> The French Council gets a lot right in this decision: it highlights that bans like this impact not just young people, but everyone online. They force people of all ages to hand over [government IDs](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/12/why-isnt-online-age-verification-just-showing-your-id-person), [face scans](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/01/face-scans-estimate-our-age-creepy-af-and-harmful), and [other sensitive information](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/06/lgbt-qa-what-data-are-companies-uk-collecting-when-verifying-my-age) into a growing surveillance ecosystem. Further, when parental consent is required, companies must collect [even more](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/05/law-should-not-require-parental-consent-all-minors-access-social-media) verification data on the parents.
